patient.chief_complaint: Confusion, agitation, and tremor 48 hours after last drink — concurrent alcoholic hepatitis on steroids
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. K. is a 48-year-old man with severe alcoholic hepatitis (Maddrey discriminant function 38) admitted 5 days ago and started on prednisolone 40 mg daily per STOPAH trial protocol. He was brought to the neurology service today from the hepatology floor for acute worsening of confusion with agitation and tremor over the past 12 hours. He last drank 48 hours before this evaluation. On admission 5 days ago he was oriented and cooperative; now he is confused, combative, and diaphoretic. His CIWA score is 12 — moderate alcohol withdrawal syndrome. The clinical picture is complicated: he has both (1) moderate alcohol withdrawal syndrome (48 hours after last drink, CIWA 12, tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, tremor, hyperreflexia), and (2) hepatic encephalopathy from his underlying alcoholic hepatitis with cirrhosis (ammonia moderately elevated, prednisolone use increasing infection risk). Both conditions can cause confusion and agitation. The prednisolone (given for alcoholic hepatitis) adds infection risk. He has no focal neurological deficits, no meningismus, and CT head is without acute changes. The CIWA score (12) is in the moderate range — treatment indicated — but benzodiazepines are relatively contraindicated in the context of concurrent HE. This is a classic moderate-difficulty HE case with a management dilemma: treating alcohol withdrawal risks worsening HE, while undertreating withdrawal risks seizures.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, grade 2-3, severe alcoholic hepatitis on steroids — concurrent moderate alcohol withdrawal syndrome (CIWA 12); hypoglycemia as critical precipitant

differential.key_features: CIWA 12, hyperreflexia, tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia — 48h after last drink; concurrent with HE; EEG excess beta consistent with withdrawal
Thiamine 28 nmol/L (deficient) in alcoholic with malnutrition — treat empirically with IV thiamine despite no ophthalmoplegia or MRI changes; cannot exclude early Wernicke
Glucose is LOW (62-64), not high — prednisolone causes hyperglycemia but this patient has liver failure impaired gluconeogenesis causing hypoglycemia instead
Leukocytosis 18.6 — but prednisolone causes leukocytosis (demargination); no clear infection source identified; blood cultures pending

optimal_actions.action: URGENT: IV thiamine 500 mg BEFORE dextrose — glucose 62-64 is hypoglycemic; thiamine-deficient alcoholic; Wernicke risk
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Thiamine 28 — deficient; glucose corrected after thiamine

optimal_actions.action: IV dextrose (D50W) + continuous D10W infusion after thiamine
CT head — exclude hemorrhage despite coagulopathy (INR 2.4)
EEG — characterize encephalopathy, note mixed HE + withdrawal pattern
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mixed theta-delta + beta overlay — HE + alcohol withdrawal

optimal_actions.action: Electrolyte repletion: IV magnesium, KCl, phosphorus
CIWA protocol with low-dose lorazepam for alcohol withdrawal; concurrent lactulose + rifaximin for HE
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Both HE and alcohol withdrawal treated

critical_actions: Hypoglycemia (glucose 62-64) is immediately life-threatening — correcting glucose before identifying it would cause neurological injury; IV thiamine FIRST then dextrose
Alcohol withdrawal seizures risk: hypomagnesemia lowers seizure threshold further — magnesium repletion is critical before withholding benzodiazepines
Concurrent HE + alcohol withdrawal requires simultaneous treatment — each is independently life-threatening; the Lille score determines steroid response
Protein restriction is CONTRAINDICATED in HE management — modern standard is adequate protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day) to support liver regeneration
contraindicated_actions: Dextrose before thiamine in thiamine-deficient alcoholic
Protein restriction in HE — outdated practice; increases mortality
Diazepam or chlordiazepoxide for alcohol withdrawal in cirrhosis
Stopping prednisolone without calculating Lille score at day 7
key_reasoning_points: Hypoglycemia in alcoholic hepatitis is a critical emergency — liver failure impairs gluconeogenesis; always check glucose in alcoholic encephalopathy
Alcohol withdrawal and HE are not mutually exclusive — they can and do coexist; the EEG mixed pattern (slow background + excess beta) reflects this duality
Protein restriction in HE is an outdated concept — ammonia production from gut bacteria can be reduced by lactulose without dietary protein restriction
Lille score at day 7 predicts steroid response in alcoholic hepatitis — score <0.45 = responder (continue steroids); >0.45 = non-responder (stop steroids)

red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose as systemic infection/sepsis as cause of encephalopathy; initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics; delay HE treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Leukocytosis >15 is an expected side effect of prednisolone (demargination of neutrophils) — not necessarily infection; blood cultures should be sent but prednisolone-related leukocytosis does not require empiric antibiotics without other signs of infection

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute all confusion to alcohol withdrawal only; treat with benzodiazepines and miss HE component; potentially over-sedate
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: CIWA 12 is significant and requires treatment, but ammonia 82 + low albumin + triphasic-like waves indicate concurrent HE; both require treatment; benzodiazepines should be minimized due to HE risk
